metadata.title: Both Sides of the Table.
metadata.greeting_note: hello lexicon: Sawadee (Thai), one word — fresh for this channel (Namaste, Kumusta, Sawubona, Hej, Merhaba, Jambo, Vanakkam and Annyeong are spent on the eight prior reels). IN-FOR-BEAR LAW in its Yatra form: Bella is the STAND-IN VOICE on Yatra's own @Yatra channel, so the greeting slot carries the NARRATOR's name, B00's first breath says the voice out loud, and the outro signs off the same way. Footer chip stays @Yatra. Voice: Kokoro af_bella (free, local).
metadata.color_semantics: Fidelity claude palette. ONE terracotta #D97757 event per beat, and it always marks THE DISTRUST — the share who walked away, the share who don't believe the process is fair, the hidden instructions. Adoption figures render in plain ink: the accent belongs to the reel's actual subject (nobody trusts the result), not to the adoption curve. Source lines ALWAYS stay muted ink — a citation is provenance, never emphasis.
metadata.note: ILLUSTRATE LAW: the Claude UI appears at B00 (cold open, ask lands ANSWERED), B04 (ask micro-beat of the one ask→result pair, resolved by B05), B11 (verdict artifact), B12 (handoff), B13 (outro). Every other beat illustrates with a purpose-built Tbl* scene. SOURCING (hard, per the human): seven figures were supplied with their citations and must be rendered VERBATIM and cited on screen. Every Tbl* scene that renders a figure REQUIRES a `source` string, so a statistic cannot reach the screen uncited, and `value` is typed as a string printed verbatim — never parsed, never recomputed, never converted between forms ('4 in 5' stays '4 in 5'). A separate numeric `bar` prop drives any drawing, so the house num() helper never has to read a value string. NO FIGURE APPEARS THAT WAS NOT SUPPLIED.

beats.narration_text: Hello, this is Bella, in for Yatra. Job hunting is now a standoff between two machines — one screening you out, one helping you past it. And nobody trusts the result.

show.event: Cream page, serif greeting 'Sawadee, Bella' above the composer — the app greets the narrator, the footer chip stays @Yatra
The ask types itself in
Terracotta send arms — the ONE accent
Three result lines stagger in; the third names the trust problem — the ask lands ANSWERED

props.command: Hiring has become AI on both sides — companies screening with it, candidates using it to get past the screening. Walk me through what each side is actually doing and whether anyone trusts the outcome. Cite every figure on screen and add none of your own.
output: the employers: 86% of organizations now use AI somewhere in hiring
the candidates: 4 in 5 job seekers use AI in their search
the result: only 26% of applicants trust AI to evaluate them fairly

beats.narration_text: Here's the whole thing in one breath. Companies screen with AI. Candidates apply with AI. Neither side trusts the process — and a human decision is getting hard to find in the middle.

show.event: Claim one sets in serif with a growing ink rule: 'Companies screen with AI.'
Claim two sets beneath, mirrored to the right: 'Candidates apply with AI.'
Claim three sets centred and lands in TERRACOTTA: 'Neither side trusts it.'
Closer lands beneath the stack: 'Nobody in this is confident.'

data.slideMeta: The whole standoff, before any figure

beats.narration_text: Start with the employers. Gartner, via CI CoPilot, puts it at eighty-six percent of organisations now using AI somewhere in hiring. Somewhere — that word is doing a lot of work.

show.event: The employer side of the frame establishes with its heading; the candidate side stays empty and faint — this beat owns one side only
The figure sets large and verbatim: 86%
Its bar fills to match — driven by a separate numeric prop, never parsed from the figure string
The qualifier sets beneath: 'somewhere in the hiring process'
Source line in muted ink: Gartner, via CI CoPilot, October 2026

data.head: The company's AI
data.label: of organizations now use AI somewhere in their hiring process
data.note: This is adoption, not outcome. It says the tools are in the room.

beats.narration_text: Now the other side. Greenhouse, also via CI CoPilot, finds four in five job seekers use AI in their search. So the screening is automated, and so is the applying.

show.event: The frame mirrors: the candidate side establishes, the employer side now holds its filled bar faintly as context
The figure sets large and VERBATIM as supplied: '4 in 5' — never converted to a percentage
Its bar fills from a separate numeric prop
The qualifier sets beneath: 'use AI in their job search'
Source line in muted ink: Greenhouse, via CI CoPilot, October 2026

data.head: The candidate's AI
data.label: job seekers now use AI in their job search
data.qualifier: use AI in their job search
data.note: Both sides automated the same year. Neither told the other.

beats.narration_text: Which means the thing in the middle isn't really a conversation. I wanted both sides drawn.

show.event: Composer returns with the generation prompt already arriving
Terracotta send arms
Running indicator reads 'drawing the table…' — the result is the next beat

props.command: Draw a hiring table with four seats: the company and its screening AI on one side, the candidate and their AI on the other. Show the two AIs exchanging with each other while both humans wait. No numbers — the arrangement is the point.

beats.narration_text: And here it is. The company's AI on one side, the candidate's AI on the other, a person on each side waiting to hear back. The systems are talking. The people aren't.

show.event: The table draws across the middle of the frame
Two seats fill on the left — the company, and its screening AI nearer the table
Two seats fill on the right — the candidate, and their AI nearer the table
Traffic starts running BETWEEN the two AI seats and keeps running — they are the only pair exchanging anything
The two human seats are pushed back from the table and dim slightly, still fully legible
A TERRACOTTA line sets beneath: 'The humans are waiting to hear back.'

data.slideMeta: Who is actually in the conversation
data.title: Four seats, one exchange
data.verdict: The humans are waiting to hear back.
data.note: This isn't AI replacing hiring. It's AI on both sides of it.

beats.narration_text: It's reached the interview. Greenhouse found sixty-three percent of job seekers have been interviewed by an AI — up thirteen points in six months. It's arriving very fast.

show.event: The figure sets large and verbatim: 63%
Its label sets: 'have been interviewed by an AI'
A short track draws below showing the six-month move, with only the DELTA labelled — the earlier value is not shown, because it was not supplied
The delta chip lands: '+13 points in six months'
Source line in muted ink: Greenhouse, May 2026

data.label: of job seekers have been interviewed by an AI
data.deltaNote: Only the change was published — the earlier figure is not shown here because it wasn't supplied.
data.note: Arriving faster than most hiring teams have written a policy for.

beats.narration_text: And people are opting out. In the same research, thirty-eight percent walked away from a hiring process because it involved an AI interview. They didn't lose. They left.

show.event: A row of applicant marks sets across the frame, all in ink
On 'thirty-eight percent', that share of the marks turns TERRACOTTA and moves OUT of the row — the motion is leaving, not being filtered
The figure sets beside them, verbatim: 38%
Label sets: 'walked away from a hiring process because it involved an AI interview'
The closing distinction lands: 'Not rejected. Withdrawn.' Source in muted ink: Greenhouse, May 2026

data.label: walked away from a hiring process entirely because it involved an AI interview
data.note: A screening tool that loses candidates before it screens them is a strange kind of filter.

beats.narration_text: Now the trust problem. Only twenty-six percent of applicants trust AI to evaluate them fairly. And Pew found sixty-six percent of US adults wouldn't want to apply at all if AI is used in the decision.

show.event: Left figure sets verbatim with its own bar and its own source: 26% trust AI to evaluate them fairly
The empty remainder of that bar is left visibly unfilled and UNLABELLED — the other 74% is arithmetic, not a published figure, so it is never captioned
Right figure sets verbatim with its own bar and its own separate source: 66% would not want to apply
Both land in TERRACOTTA — this beat is the reel's subject, so the accent covers the pair
Two distinct source lines sit beneath their own figures in muted ink — the figures come from different studies and are never merged

data.slideMeta: What people think of the process
data.title: Two different studies, one direction

left.label: of applicants trust AI to evaluate them fairly

right.label: of US adults would not want to apply for a job if AI is used in the hiring decision

data.note: Different samples, different questions. They are shown side by side, not added together.

beats.narration_text: So candidates fight the machine directly. SelectSoftwareReviews found forty-one percent admit to hiding prompt injections or instructions in their resumes — text written for the screening AI, not for a person.

show.event: A resume page draws, perfectly ordinary, ink on white
On 'hidden instructions', a second layer fades up INSIDE the page — text that was always there and simply wasn't visible
The hidden layer renders in TERRACOTTA and is addressed to the machine, not the reader
The figure sets beside the page, verbatim: 41%
Label and source set in muted ink: SelectSoftwareReviews, 2026. The chip reads ADMIT TO — this is self-reported

data.label: of job candidates admit to using prompt injections or hidden instructions in their resumes to bypass AI screening
data.hiddenLabel: written for the screening AI, not for a reader
data.note: The arms race stopped being a metaphor somewhere around here.

beats.narration_text: Worth being exact. These are separate studies with separate samples. A self-reported figure is what people admit to. And none of this says AI makes worse hires — only that neither side trusts the process.

show.event: Left ledger heads WHAT THE FIGURES SHOW and three lines stack in
Right ledger heads WHAT THEY DON'T and its lines stack in TERRACOTTA — the accent sits on the refusals, where the honesty is
A muted provenance rule draws across the foot listing all four sources behind this reel
The falsifier lands last: 'Different studies. Read them before you stack them.'

data.title: What these numbers are, and aren't

claims.heading: What the figures show
items: AI is in use on both sides of hiring, widely
AI interviews are spreading fast, and some candidates refuse them
most applicants do not trust AI to judge them fairly

refusals.heading: What they don't
items: that they measure one population — these are separate studies
that self-reported behaviour is observed behaviour
that AI is making worse hires — none of these measure hire quality

data.provenance: Sources: Gartner (via CI CoPilot, Oct 2026) · Greenhouse (via CI CoPilot, Oct 2026) · Greenhouse (May 2026) · Greenhouse Candidate AI Interview Report, 2026 · Pew Research Center · SelectSoftwareReviews, 2026
data.falsifier: Different studies. Read them before you stack them.

beats.narration_text: So — the standoff. Eighty-six percent of organisations screen with AI. Four in five job seekers apply with it. Thirty-eight percent walk away from AI interviews, and only twenty-six percent think it's fair. This isn't AI replacing hiring — it's AI on both sides, with the humans waiting to find out who decided.

Line five lands and holds — the actual conclusion

props.artifactTitle: Both Sides of the Table. — the standoff
artifactLines: The employers: 86% of organizations now use AI somewhere in their hiring process (Gartner, via CI CoPilot, Oct 2026).
The candidates: 4 in 5 job seekers use AI in their job search (Greenhouse, via CI CoPilot, Oct 2026).
The interview: 63% have been interviewed by an AI, up 13 points in six months — and 38% walked away from a process because of it (Greenhouse, May 2026).

The trust: only 26% of applicants trust AI to evaluate them fairly (Greenhouse Candidate AI Interview Report, 2026); 66% of US adults would not want to apply if AI is used in the decision (Pew Research Center). 41% admit to hiding instructions in their resumes (SelectSoftwareReviews, 2026).
The conclusion: this isn't AI replacing hiring — it's AI on both sides of it, and the humans are waiting to find out who actually decided.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. If you're hiring or job hunting, paste this: tell me which steps of this process a machine is doing, which a human is doing, and at which exact step a person first reads my name. Look for whether it can find that step at all.

show.event: Serif 'Your turn.' replaces the persona greeting
The prompt types itself in as the narration reads it aloud, verbatim
Terracotta send arms
Three-item rubric stacks in as each check is discussed
